title: Lends and lexical borrowing
description: Ownership, explicit mut, projections as inline callbacks, @law disjoint, and why borrows never escape their block.

exercises.title: Spell the mutation
exercises.prompt: Given fn bump(mut xs: [V]Int, by: Int), which call adds 1 to every element of the caller's array a?
exercises.hint: A mutable borrow is written at both ends: the parameter and the call.
exercises.solution: bump(mut a, 1). The parameter says mut xs and the call says mut a, so every line that can change a visibly contains mut a.
options: bump(a, 1)
bump(a.copy(), 1)
bump(mut a, 1)
bump(&mut a, 1)
exercises.explanation: bump(a, 1) and bump(a.copy(), 1) both omit the required mut and are rejected. An explicit owned copy would not change a anyway. &mut is Rust syntax; CP Lang has no reference operator.
exercises.code:
fn bump(mut xs: [V]Int, by: Int):
    for v in V: xs[v] += by

exercises.title: Why a projection cannot dangle
exercises.prompt: fn at(mut self, i: V) lends mut Int ends with the tail expression mut self.cnt[i]. Why can the caller never keep a dangling reference to cnt[i]?
exercises.hint: Think about what c.at(v) += 5 desugars to, and where that code runs.
exercises.solution: A projection is sugar for fn at(mut self, i: V, use: (mut Int) -> R) -> R = use(mut self.cnt[i]), with the callback inlined. The rest of the caller's expression is the callback, it runs while at is still on the stack, and nothing reference-like is ever returned.
options: The caller's expression runs as an inlined callback inside at, so the borrow ends before at returns
The runtime reference-counts every cell of cnt
The checker infers a lifetime parameter for the returned reference
The projection copies cnt[i], so there is no reference at all
exercises.explanation: There is no reference counting and no lifetime inference: the design avoids both. A projection does not copy; c.at(v) += 5 really changes cnt[v], which is the point of a mutable projection.

exercises.title: Prove the law at the call
exercises.prompt: Bag.at declares @law disjoint(i, j) = i != j, and Bag.other is a second projection that also lends cnt[i]. Which call does the checker accept?
exercises.hint: The law only relates two lends of the same projection, and the fact must be visible before the call.
exercises.solution: The guarded call through the same projection. The enclosing if gives the checker i != j, which is exactly the law of at, so the two mutable lends cannot overlap.
options: move(mut b.at(i), mut b.at(j)) with nothing known about i and j
if i != j: move(mut b.at(i), mut b.other(j))
move(mut b.at(i), mut b.at(i)) followed by assert i != j
if i != j: move(mut b.at(i), mut b.at(j))
exercises.explanation: Without the guard nothing proves i != j, so the call is rejected with help to guard or assert. Different projections (at and other) are never assumed disjoint, even when i != j. An assert after the call is too late, and lending b.at(i) twice can never satisfy i != j.

exercises.title: Return the window, not the slice
exercises.prompt: A helper should find the best segment of a, and the caller then sorts that segment in place. Which design fits CP Lang's borrowing rules?
exercises.hint: A slice is a borrow; a range is a plain value.
exercises.solution: Return Range<V> and re-project at the point of use: sort(mut a[w]). The range can be stored, returned, or pushed anywhere, and the borrow is created only where the caller applies it.
options: fn best(a: [V]Int) -> [V]Int returning a[l..=r]
fn best(a: [V]Int) -> Range<V> returning l..=r, then sort(mut a[best(a)])
Store a[l..=r] in a struct field and sort it later
Assign a[l..=r] to a var and return the var
exercises.explanation: Returning a slice, storing it in a field, or assigning it to a var would each let the borrow outlive its block, and all three are rejected with help to keep the range or call .copy(). A copy compiles too, but sorting a copy would not change a.

exercises.title: Trace a lends mut projection
exercises.prompt: lends.cp starts cnt at all zeros, applies q updates through c.at(pos) += delta, then calls add_all(mut c.cnt, 1). Predict the printed array for each input.
exercises.hint: Apply each (pos, delta) update to 1-based slot pos, then add 1 to every slot.
exercises.solution: Case 1: [0, 0, 0] -> [5, 0, -2] -> [6, 1, -1]. Case 2: [0, 0] -> [0, 10] -> [1, 11]. Case 3: [0] -> [9] -> [10]. Both c.at(pos) += delta and add_all(mut c.cnt, 1) mutate in place with no copies.

exercises.title: Update through a mutable projection
exercises.prompt: Read n and q. All n counters start at 0. Each of the q updates gives a position and a signed delta. Apply the updates through Counter.at and print the final counters in position order.
exercises.hint: Inside the update loop, write c.at(pos) += delta. The lend ends after that statement.
exercises.solution: Counter.at projects the chosen array cell as lends mut Int. A compound assignment changes that cell in place without storing or returning a borrow.

title: Tropical Optionals and @memo DP
description: Eliminate INF sentinels with niche-packed ?T, tropical min=/max=, lazy ??=, and cached @memo recurrences.

exercises.title: Trace tropical coin change
exercises.prompt: tropical_dp.cp initializes dp: [0..=x]?Int = none, sets dp[0] = 0, relaxes dp[s] min= dp[s - c] + 1, and prints dp[x] ?? -1. Predict the output for each input.
exercises.hint: If no combination of coins reaches sum x, dp[x] stays none and ?? -1 prints -1.
exercises.solution: For coins [1, 5, 7] and x = 11: 5 + 5 + 1 uses 3 coins (better than 7 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 5). For coins [2, 4] and x = 3: odd sum is unreachable, so dp[3] is none and prints -1. For coins [2, 3] and x = 6: 3 + 3 uses 2 coins.

exercises.title: Track max= and ??=
exercises.prompt: optional_coalesce.cp scans a, updates best_even max= x for even values, and runs first_neg ??= x for negative values. Predict the two printed numbers for each input.
exercises.hint: max= keeps the largest even number seen; ??= writes only when first_neg is still none, so it keeps the first negative number.
exercises.solution: Case 1: evens are -4, -2, 6 (max 6); first negative is -4 -> 6 -4. Case 2: no evens and no negatives -> fallbacks -1 0. Case 3: evens -8, -2 (max -2); first negative -8 -> -2 -8.

exercises.title: Which optional operation is rejected?
exercises.prompt: Given var x: ?Int = 1 and var y: ?Int = none, which statement does CP Lang reject at compile time?
exercises.hint: Arithmetic/bitwise expressions and min=/max= lift over ?Int, but compound += / -= do not.
exercises.solution: x += 2 is rejected (E0309). Compound +=, -=, ?V + k, and sum(...) never lift over ?Int; write x = x + 2 or unwrap first.
options: y min= x + 3
let z = x ?? 0
exercises.explanation: y min= x + 3 is valid tropical DP, y ??= 5 lazily initializes y, and x ?? 0 unwraps with a fallback. x += 2 is intentionally rejected with E0309 because += is not a tropical update.

exercises.title: Predict the @memo recurrence
exercises.prompt: memo_dp.cp caches ways(k) = ways(k - 1) + ways(k - 2) with ways(0) = ways(1) = 1. Predict the output for n = 1, 5, and 10.
exercises.hint: The sequence starts ways(0)=1, ways(1)=1, ways(2)=2, ways(3)=3, ways(4)=5, ways(5)=8, ...
exercises.solution: ways(1) = 1, ways(5) = 8, and ways(10) = 89. Because @memo caches every state in a flat table, even ways(35) runs instantaneously in WebAssembly.

exercises.title: When @memo caches reset
exercises.prompt: A @memo fn dp(i: V) -> Int is declared below @!multitest and reads the per-test array a. What happens when the second test case starts?
exercises.hint: Think about what @!multitest guarantees for everything below the divider.
exercises.solution: The @memo cache is cleared automatically at the start of every test case (and every iteration if nested in a loop), so stale answers from test 1 never leak into test 2.
options: The cache keeps entries from test 1 unless you call dp.clear()
The cache resets automatically for every test case below @!multitest
@memo cannot be used below @!multitest
You must pass the test case index t as an extra parameter to dp
exercises.explanation: Automatic per-test and per-loop resets are a core 0.2.2 rule that removes one of the most common multitest WA bugs without manual memset or generation counters.

exercises.title: Complete the optional coin-change DP
exercises.prompt: Read n, a target x, and n positive coin values. You may use each coin any number of times. Print the fewest coins needed to reach exactly x, or -1 if it is impossible. Target 0 needs 0 coins.
exercises.hint: Set dp[0] = 0. For each sum s and coin c <= s, relax dp[s] min= dp[s - c] + 1.
exercises.solution: Unreachable sums stay none. Adding 1 to none stays none, and min= ignores that candidate. Reachable candidates compete by coin count.

title: Algebraic segment trees and Rooted
description: Bare operators, Monoid(id, op), Action(id, compose, apply, over), SegTree, LazySegTree, and Rooted<V> tree paths.

exercises.title: Trace SegTree with Monoid
exercises.prompt: segtree_monoid.cp builds SegTree<V, Int> from Monoid<Int>(0, +). Type 1 sets pos to val; type 2 prints the inclusive range sum fold(l..=r). Predict the outputs.
exercises.hint: Track the array after each type-1 point update, then sum l..=r on each type-2 query.

exercises.title: Trace LazySegTree with Action
exercises.prompt: lazy_action.cp uses Action<Int, Int> for range add and range sum. Type 1 adds d to l..=r; type 2 prints fold(l..=r). Predict the outputs.
exercises.hint: Adding d to a range of length span increases its sum by d * span.

exercises.title: Predict the fold
exercises.prompt: a.sum() is a fold of + starting from the identity 0. Predict the output of this runnable program for each input.
exercises.hint: Write the fold out as ((0 + x1) + x2) + ..., and remember that adding 0 changes nothing.
exercises.solution: The fold starts at the identity 0 and adds each element: 0 + 5 - 2 + 4 = 7; -3 + 3 = 0; and a single element is just itself, -9, because 0 + x == x.

exercises.title: Which combine can a segment tree use?
exercises.prompt: A segment tree regroups pieces freely. Which combine gives correct range answers however the query splits?
exercises.hint: Check (x op y) op z against x op (y op z) on three small numbers.
exercises.solution: max is associative, max(max(x, y), z) == max(x, max(y, z)), with identity Int.MIN, so it is a monoid and any grouping gives the same answer.
options: (a, b) => max(a, b)
(a, b) => a - b
(a, b) => keep whichever piece was combined first on a tie, else the larger
exercises.explanation: Averaging is not associative: avg(avg(2, 4), 6) = 4.5 but avg(2, avg(4, 6)) = 3.5; carry (sum, count) instead. Subtraction is not associative either. A rule that depends on combination history gives answers that depend on how the query happens to split across nodes.

exercises.title: When two prefix values are enough
exercises.prompt: Which range query can always be answered from two prefix values, prefix(r) combined with the inverse of prefix(l - 1)?
exercises.hint: Taking a prefix back out needs an inverse operation.
exercises.solution: Range sum: + has the inverse -, so sum(l..=r) = pre[r.r] - pre[l.l]. That is why Fenwick<D, Int> is sum-only while arbitrary monoids belong in SegTree.
options: Range maximum
Range minimum
Range gcd
Range sum
exercises.explanation: Maximum, minimum, and gcd have no inverse: knowing max(1..=r) and max(1..=l-1) tells you nothing about max(l..=r). Use SegTree<V, Int>(max, a) or SparseTable<V, Int>(min, a) for those; Fenwick<V, Int>(a) stays dedicated to sums.

exercises.title: Order matters in Action.compose
exercises.prompt: An affine Action applies old_f = (3, 0) (x => 3x) first, then new_f = (2, 1) (x => 2x + 1). What is compose(new_f, old_f)?
exercises.hint: Substitute 3x into 2(...) + 1 and expand.
exercises.solution: Applying old_f first gives 3x, then new_f gives 2(3x) + 1 = 6x + 1, so compose(new_f, old_f) = (6, 1). Reversing the order gives 3(2x + 1) = 6x + 3.
exercises.explanation: (6, 3) is the reversed order, the classic bug when composing lazy tags backwards. Action.compose(new_f, old_f) always applies old_f first and new_f second.

exercises.title: Bare operators vs. Monoid(id, op)
exercises.prompt: In CP Lang 0.2.2, how do you construct a range-sum SegTree and a custom (best, count) SegTree over domain V?
exercises.hint: Standard associative operators need no wrapper; custom node combines use Monoid(id, op).
exercises.solution: Pass the bare operator + for range sums (SegTree<V, Int>(+, a)) and Monoid(id, op) for a custom combine over a node value.
options: SegTree<V, Int>(+, a) for sum, and SegTree<V, (Int, Int)>(Monoid(id, op), init) for custom nodes
Wrap + in a custom wrapper struct before passing it to SegTree
Sub-class a SegTree base class and override combine()
Pass a string "+" that SegTree parses at runtime
exercises.explanation: CP Lang 0.2.2 has no single-purpose operator wrapper types. Built-in associative operators (+, *, ^, &, |, min, max, gcd) pass directly to SegTree and SparseTable, while custom monoids pass Monoid(id, op) and lazy tags pass stock tags like AddSum or Action(id, compose, apply, over).

exercises.title: Trace Fenwick point updates and range sums
exercises.prompt: fenwick_sum.cp builds a Fenwick<V, Int> from a, handles type-1 point additions `fw.add(pos, delta)`, and prints type-2 inclusive sums `fw.sum(l..=r)`. Predict the output for each input.
exercises.hint: Type 1 adds delta to position pos (it does not overwrite). Type 2 prints the sum from l through r inclusive.

exercises.title: What a local library costs
exercises.prompt: A solution imports a structure from a large personal local library configured in cp.toml. What ends up in the compiled C++17 file?
exercises.hint: Judges accept one file and know nothing about your local folders.
exercises.solution: Only the code reachable from your solution is inlined into the single C++17 file; unused modules, `@brute` blocks, and tests are stripped.
options: The whole library folder, concatenated
An #include pointing to the library path on your machine
Only the code the solution reaches, inlined into one file and tree-shaken
Nothing until the judge downloads the library
exercises.explanation: Concatenating the whole folder would blow past judge size limits. Local `#include` paths fail on judges, and judges never fetch dependencies. Tree-shaking keeps every submission compact and self-contained.

exercises.title: Maintain range minima with SegTree
exercises.prompt: Read n, q, and n integers. Query 1 pos value replaces a value. Query 2 l r prints the minimum on the inclusive interval l..=r. Complete the two operations using the minimum monoid.
exercises.hint: Construct SegTree<V, Int>(min, a). Use st.set(pos, value) for updates and st.fold(l..=r) for queries.
exercises.solution: Minimum is associative, so a segment tree can combine adjacent pieces. Point updates replace one leaf; an inclusive range fold returns its smallest current value.

title: Graphs, trees, number theory, and geometry
description:
Use Dsu, flat CSR Graph, bfs/dijkstra, Rooted LCA and HLD, FlowGraph, Mod

, Sieve, string algorithms, and exact Pt geometry.

exercises.title: Count components and combinations
exercises.prompt: dsu_mod.cp unites m edges in a Dsu<V>, computes the number of connected components c, and prints c alongside C(n, c) modulo 1_000_000_007. Predict the output for each input.
exercises.hint: Start with n components; each edge uniting two different components reduces c by 1. Then compute n choose c.
exercises.solution: Case 1: 5 vertices with edges (1,2), (2,3), (4,5) -> 2 components ({1,2,3} and {4,5}), C(5, 2) = 10. Case 2: 4 vertices with edges (1,2), (2,3), (1,3) -> edge (1,3) is redundant, so 2 components ({1,2,3} and {4}), C(4, 2) = 6.

exercises.title:
Why Mod

does not implement Ord
exercises.prompt:
Which operation on two `Mod

` values `a` and `b` is intentionally a compile error?
exercises.hint: Modular residues wrap around P, so there is no mathematically consistent less-than order.
exercises.solution:
`a < b` is a compile error because `Mod

` does not implement `Ord`. Use `.val` explicitly if you truly want to compare raw residues in `0..P`.
options: a / b
a == b
a < b
exercises.explanation:
Modular division (`a / b`), equality (`a == b`), and exponentiation (`a ** 10`) are all well-defined on `Mod

`. Ordering (`<`, `min`, `sort`) on residues is almost always a bug — such as taking `min` of DP counts after reducing modulo P — so `Mod

` omits `Ord`.

exercises.title: Unreachable vertices in bfs and dijkstra
exercises.prompt: After running `let dist = dijkstra(g, [src])`, how do you check whether vertex `t` is reachable and print `-1` if it is not?
exercises.hint: dijkstra returns `[V]?Int` — no sentinel 1e18 needed.
exercises.solution: `print(dist[t] ?? -1)` prints the shortest distance if reachable, or `-1` when `dist[t]` is `none`.
options: print(if dist[t] >= 1e18: -1 else: dist[t])
print(dist[t] ?? -1)
print(dist[t]!)
print(max(dist[t], -1))
exercises.explanation: `dist` has type `[V]?Int`, so unreachable vertices hold `none` rather than a sentinel. `dist[t]!` traps if `t` is unreachable, and `max(dist[t], -1)` skips `none` and would print `-1` even when `dist[t]` is a valid distance smaller than `-1` (and misses the intent of fallback).

exercises.title: Why Rooted<V> exposes its own domain t.Pre
exercises.prompt: You build a segment tree `var st = SegTree<t.Pre, Int>(+, init)` over a `Rooted<V>` tree `t`. What happens if you call `st.set(u, 5)` directly with a vertex `u: V`?
options: It automatically converts u to its Euler preorder index
It compiles and silently updates the wrong position tin[u]
It is a compile-time type error because st expects t.Pre, not V
It traps at runtime only when u is not the root
exercises.hint: Check whether `u` has the index type of `st`.
exercises.solution: It is a compile-time type error because `st` is indexed by `t.Pre`, not `V`. Write `st.set(t.pos(u), 5)` to map the vertex to its Euler preorder position.
exercises.explanation: Forgetting to map `u` through `tin[u]` before querying a subtree segment tree is one of the most common tree-DP bugs in C++. Making `t.Pre` a distinct value-owned domain catches that mix-up at compile time with zero runtime cost.

exercises.title: Exact angular sorting and orientation
exercises.prompt: You need to sort 2D lattice points `Pt(x, y)` around the origin without floating-point precision errors. What does `std.geometry` provide?
options: atan2(p.y, p.x) on F64
ByAngle (half-plane + exact integer cross product) and orient(a, b, c)
Sorting by p.y / p.x with Euclidean integer division
Converting each Pt to Mod
exercises.hint: Avoid `atan2` on integers; use exact cross-product predicates.
exercises.solution: Use `ByAngle` (backed by half-plane + exact `cross` sign) and `orient(a, b, c) -> -1 | 0 | 1`, both computed in exact integer arithmetic.
exercises.explanation: `atan2` converts coordinates to `F64` and can mis-order nearly collinear points with coordinates up to 1e9. `ByAngle` and `orient` stay completely exact using 64-bit / 128-bit integer cross products.

exercises.title: Count connected components
exercises.prompt: Read n, m, and m undirected edges on vertices 1..=n. Use Dsu<V> to print the number of connected components after all edges. Repeated edges and self-loops do not create extra merges.
exercises.hint: Start with n singleton components. Call d.unite(u, v) for each edge, then print d.components.
exercises.solution: Union-find joins two components only when their representatives differ. Isolated vertices remain singleton components; duplicate edges and self-loops leave the count unchanged.

title: Co-located @brute, @checker, and @interactor
description: In-file slow oracles with @brute, constructive validators with @checker, interactive judges with @interactor, shrinking, and binary search.

exercises.title: Check fast vs. co-located @brute
exercises.prompt: colocated_brute.cp computes the maximum non-empty subarray sum in O(n) using boundary prefixes, alongside @brute(main) fn slow(). Predict the output for each input.
exercises.hint: The subarray must be non-empty, so an all-negative array returns its largest (least negative) element.
exercises.solution: Case 1: [4, -1, 3] sums to 6. Case 2: all negative [-5, -2, -8], best single element is -2. Case 3: all positive [1, 2, 3, 4], whole array sums to 10.

exercises.title: What makes a good brute
exercises.prompt: You suspect range_sum, which uses a prefix table. Which @brute(range_sum) is most useful?
exercises.hint: A brute should be too simple to share the fast version's bug.
exercises.solution: The direct loop. It is obviously correct, it checks exactly the suspect function, and cpl stress shrinks to the first failing case, such as l=1 r=1.
options: A copy of range_sum with different variable names
A brute for the whole program that also uses the prefix table
No brute: compare against the sample output only
sum(a[i] for i in l..=r), a direct loop over the range
exercises.explanation: A renamed copy shares every bug. A whole-program brute built on the same prefix table shares the idea and only says the final answer differs. Samples are a handful of cases, while cpl stress tries thousands of generated inputs and shrinks the first counterexample.

exercises.title: A good shrink step
exercises.prompt: A stress failure has n = 37, twelve queries, and the constraint l <= r on each query. Which step does the planned structure-aware shrinker take?
exercises.hint: Every candidate must stay a valid input and must reproduce the same bug.
exercises.solution: It deletes a query (or an element, or lowers a value) while keeping every constraint true, and accepts the candidate only if it fails at the same first differing stage or crash line.
options: Delete random bytes from the input file
Remove one query, and keep the smaller case only if it still fails the same way
Swap l and r in a query to make the first number smaller
Keep any smaller case that fails for any reason
exercises.explanation: Byte deletion produces invalid input. Swapping l and r can break l <= r. Accepting any failure lets the shrinker drift to a different bug than the one you are chasing.

exercises.title: Who decides existence
exercises.prompt: With a co-located @checker for a print-any-valid-coloring problem, the brute prints -1 because no coloring exists. When does your output pass?
exercises.hint: The checker judges an answer; something else settles whether an answer exists.
exercises.solution: Only -1 passes. The brute settles existence; when it does find an answer, your output must parse as [V]Color and pass valid. The checker never needs to decide whether a coloring exists, which keeps it short.
options: Only when your output is also -1
When valid(c) returns true for your coloring
Whenever your output parses as [V]Color
When your output equals the brute's output character for character
exercises.explanation: Printing a coloring when none exists is wrong, so valid is not even consulted. Parsing is necessary but not sufficient. Character-for-character comparison is exactly what checkers replace.

exercises.title: Fit the query limit
exercises.prompt: An interactive problem has a secret in 1..=1e9 and allows at most 30 queries via ask("?", x, limit: 30) paired with @interactor. Which strategy fits the budget for every secret?
exercises.hint: Count how many halvings it takes to get from 10^9 candidates to one.
exercises.solution: Binary search with bsearch_first(1..=1e9, ok) needs at most 30 asks, because 2^30 is just over 10^9. Locally, @interactor enforces limit: 30 and prints the query transcript if a 31st is made.
options: Ask every value from 1 upward
Ask 30 random values and answer the closest
Binary search with bsearch_first(1..=1e9, ok), about log2(1e9) questions
Ternary search with two asks per step
exercises.explanation: A linear scan needs up to 10^9 asks. Random asks are not correct. Ternary search with two asks per step needs about 2 * log base 1.5 of 10^9, roughly 100, far more than 30.

exercises.title: Predict the linear recurrence
exercises.prompt: f(0) = 1 and f(i) = f(i - 1) * 3 + i. Predict the output of memo.cp (which prints f(n - 1)) for each n.
exercises.hint: 0..n is half-open, so the last index is n - 1. Build the values upward from f(0).
exercises.solution: The sequence is f(0) = 1, f(1) = 4, f(2) = 14, f(3) = 45, f(4) = 139, and the program prints f(n - 1). So n = 1 prints 1, n = 3 prints 14, and n = 5 prints 139.

exercises.title: Repair an all-negative counterexample
exercises.prompt: The fast program incorrectly allows an empty subarray and prints 0 for all-negative input. Fix it to print the maximum sum of a nonempty contiguous subarray. Keep the co-located brute for comparison; Trace can compare the two programs on the editable input.
exercises.hint: Initialize from an actual array element, not 0. At each later element, choose between starting a new subarray and extending the current one.
exercises.solution: Starting at the first element enforces nonemptiness. The running sum is the best subarray ending here, and best is the largest running sum so far. The brute enumerates every nonempty interval.
